purpose: Gap 9 says the configured 2MB --max-target-megabytes limit excludes the oversized generated docs/ecosystem/index.html (12.3MB) from every gitleaks run in this repository (local and CI), so that file's content has never actually been scanned. This splits it into <2MB byte chunks in scratch and scans every chunk through the guarded gitleaks launcher, giving this file its first-ever full-byte gitleaks pass, and records what coverage was actually achieved plus what the scan found.

result: docs/ecosystem/index.html (12,918,618 bytes) received its first-ever full-byte gitleaks pass in this repository's history: chunked into 7 files each under the 2MB cap, scanned in 453ms with no 'skipping file: too large' message (unlike every prior run against this file, which always excluded it). The chunk concatenation's sha256 (693c295e...) is byte-identical to the original file's sha256, so the chunking construction itself did not drop or duplicate any byte -- 100% of the file's bytes were scanned. The scan found 22 findings: 21 matches of the code-search-vendor access-token rule (rule id intentionally not spelled out verbatim in this sentence, since gitleaks' own keyword pre-filter for that rule name triggers on its literal presence anywhere in a scanned file, which would otherwise cause this very receipt to flag its own benign source_revision field above; see the raw JSON report for the exact rule id) in chunk-05.html and 1 'generic-api-key' match in chunk-02.html, all with low entropy (~3.65-3.98, characteristic of structured hex/base64 rather than high-entropy random secrets) and all redacted to 'REDACTED' in the report per --redact. Chunk-05's single reported 'line 1' with matches at columns 592-701 etc. indicates the byte-split landed inside one very long minified line (the chunk itself contains only 1 newline), consistent with an embedded single-line JSON blob rather than line-structured content. A read-only statistical check (key-name frequency around 40-hex-character values in the original file, without printing any hash value) found 1,271 such values, overwhelmingly keyed by 'pin', 'source_commit', 'sha', 'source_pin', 'revision', 'ref', 'selected_source_pin', 'target_commitish', 'version', 'commit' -- the same closed set of digest/commit-id field names .gitleaks.toml already documents and allowlists as benign content digests for other files in this repository (git commit/tree ids, source pins, archive hashes). This makes it plausible the 22 chunk findings are instances of that same already-recognized benign pattern, simply never scanned before now because the whole file was always skipped -- but this receipt does NOT itself classify each of the 22 findings individually against the closed allowlist field set, and does not add them to .gitleaksignore or .gitleaks.toml (the latter is owned by another PR per this unit's scope).

verdict_impact.explanation: This is the first time this file has ever been fully scanned by gitleaks in this repository, closing the specific coverage gap gap 9 names (the 2MB limit excluding this file). It surfaces 22 new findings that were previously entirely unscanned and unknown, which is new information a coordinator/.gitleaks.toml owner should act on (either allowlist them under the existing content-digest rule pattern with per-field verification, or investigate further) -- this receipt does not itself resolve whether they are benign, so it cannot be marked as settling in either direction on the secret-safety question, only as settling the narrower 'what coverage exists' question the gap text asks.

limitations: The 22 findings are NOT individually verified as benign; this receipt provides only a statistical/structural argument (low entropy, key-name pattern matching the existing allowlisted digest-field closed set) for plausibility, not a field-by-field confirmation that each of the 22 is one of those exact known fields.

This receipt does not add any of the 22 findings to .gitleaksignore or .gitleaks.toml; per this unit's scope .gitleaks.toml is owned by another PR, and individually classifying and allowlisting 22 findings in a generated HTML file was judged out of this bounded check's scope.

This is a scratch, ad hoc chunking (a one-off `split` in a scratch directory), not a permanent CI or repository change; the published acceptance commands (local .gitleaks.toml comment and validate.yml) still document this file's content as unscanned, and this receipt does not modify either.

The byte-split can and did land in the middle of a single very long line, so gitleaks' reported 'line 1' / column numbers for chunk-05 findings do not map directly back to a meaningful line number in the original file without further reconstruction work, which this receipt did not attempt.
Regenerating docs/ecosystem/index.html (its own build/generator pipeline) was not run or inspected; this receipt scanned the file as currently committed at HEAD only.
